line.title: Line
line.hook: A line can do a job before anyone reads a word.
line.goal: Find how a line divides, connects, outlines, or guides.

types.label: Horizontal
types.input: The line runs from left to right.

types.label: Vertical
types.input: The line runs from top to bottom.

types.label: Diagonal
types.input: The line slopes across the picture.

types.label: Curved
types.input: The path bends instead of staying straight.

types.label: Dashed
types.input: Small gaps break the line into separate marks.

types.label: Implied
types.input: Separate dots suggest a path without a continuous stroke.

vocab.meaning: How thick or thin a line is.
The way a line runs.
The line around the edge of a shape.
A line that separates information.
A line around the outside of a design.
A path that leads the eye.

lab.label: Change the line weight
lab.observation: The path stays in the same place. Only its thickness changes.

check.question: What does the horizontal rule do in this timetable?
choices: It separates the two sessions.
It changes the starting time.
It adds a new room.
check.reason: The rule separates the two sessions while the wording stays the same.

line.extension: A heavy line can compete with information. Choose a weight that supports the message, then check it at the final viewing size.

color.title: Color
color.hook: A color can identify a group or make one detail stand out.
color.goal: Separate the color itself from its intensity and lightness.

types.label: Hue
types.input: Orange, yellow, green, blue, purple: the color family changes.

types.label: Saturation
types.input: The same hue changes from muted to vivid.

types.label: Value / lightness
types.input: The same hue changes from dark to light.

types.label: Monochromatic
types.input: The colors share one hue but have different lightness.

types.label: Analogous
types.input: The hues sit beside each other on this digital color wheel.

types.label: Complementary
types.input: The two hues sit opposite each other on this digital wheel.

types.label: Triadic
types.input: Three hues are evenly spaced around the digital wheel.

vocab.meaning: The color family, such as orange, green, or blue.
How vivid or muted a color appears.
How light or dark a color appears.
A color made lighter by adding white.
A color made darker by adding black.
The selected colors used together.

lab.label: Change saturation
lab.observation: The hue and lightness stay fixed. The color becomes more or less vivid.

check.question: Why can a color key help a reader use this club timetable?
choices: The color and written labels identify different activities.
Every activity has changed its time.
Bright colors always mean the same thing everywhere.
check.reason: The colors repeat beside the activity names. The written labels give a second cue, so color is not the only way to identify an activity.

color.extension: A palette does not guarantee readable text. Check light–dark difference separately. Meanings associated with colors depend on audience and context; ask rather than assume.

shape.title: Shape
shape.hook: A shape is a flat area with a boundary. It can be drawn, filled, or cut out.
shape.goal: Compare geometric and organic shapes without confusing shape with volume.

types.label: Geometric
types.input: Circles, squares, and triangles have regular geometric structures.

types.label: Organic
types.input: The irregular outlines resemble forms found in nature.

types.label: Outline
types.input: A line describes the boundary; the middle is unfilled.

types.label: Solid
types.input: The flat area inside the boundary is filled.

types.label: Cut-out
types.input: The empty shape is visible inside a filled area.

vocab.meaning: The edge that separates a shape from its surroundings.
A point where two edges meet.
Built from regular geometry, such as a circle or square.
An irregular shape with a less rigid outline.
The outer shape seen as one flat area.
An empty area removed from a filled shape.

lab.label: Round the corners
lab.observation: The outline changes, but the shape is still a flat area.

check.question: Which feature makes these simple activity icons easy to tell apart?
choices: Their different outlines.
Their hidden file names.
Their three-dimensional mass.
check.reason: You can distinguish the circle, square, and triangle by their outlines. They are flat shapes.

shape.extension: Shape associations are interpretations, not universal meanings. A curved shape may seem softer in one context, but the audience and the rest of the design matter.

texture.title: Texture
texture.hook: A flat illustration can make a surface look rough, smooth, or woven.
texture.goal: Identify the visual surface and distinguish a texture from a physical touch.

types.label: Wood grain
types.input: Irregular flowing lines suggest the grain of wood.

types.label: Rough stone
types.input: Uneven marks suggest a rough, mottled surface.

types.label: Woven fabric
types.input: Crossing threads form a regular weave.

types.label: Smooth surface
types.input: Few surface marks make this illustration look smooth.

types.label: Repeating pattern
types.input: The same motif repeats in a regular arrangement.

vocab.meaning: The lines and changes visible in a material such as wood.
A surface that appears uneven.
A surface that appears even, with few irregular marks.
Made from threads crossing over and under each other.
One visual unit that repeats.
Texture suggested by an image; you cannot feel the illustrated surface through the screen.

lab.label: Change texture strength
lab.observation: The illustration keeps the same outline. Its surface marks become more noticeable.

check.question: What should you check before placing small text over this textured invitation?
choices: Whether the surface marks compete with the words.
Whether the screen feels like wood.
Whether texture changes the event date.
check.reason: A strong texture can compete with small text. A quieter area behind the words can help readability.

texture.extension: Texture may suggest a material or tone, but it is also visual detail. Keep its strength appropriate to the message and check small lettering against it.

space.title: Space
space.hook: Space is occupied area and empty area. Empty space does not have to be white.
space.goal: Use gaps to separate information and understand inside, outside, and between.

types.label: Positive space
types.input: The filled shape occupies space.

types.label: Negative space
types.input: The empty area around and inside the shape helps define it.

types.label: Margin
types.input: The gap lies between the page edge and its content.

types.label: Padding
types.input: The gap lies inside a panel, around its content.

types.label: Gutter
types.input: The gap separates two columns.

types.label: Overlap
types.input: One shape partly covers another, suggesting a front and a back.

vocab.meaning: Area occupied by a visible element.
The empty area inside, around, or between elements.
Space between the outer edge and content.
Space inside a panel around its content.
Space between columns.
One element covering part of another.

lab.label: Change the gap around the heading
lab.observation: The words stay the same. More or less empty area separates the heading from the details.

check.question: What does the empty gap between these timetable columns help show?
choices: That the columns are separate groups.
That the timetable has no content.
That all empty space must be white.
check.reason: The gutter separates the columns. It contains the same background color as the page, but it is still empty space.

space.extension: Spacing affects grouping, emphasis, and comfort. Large gaps can separate related details too much; choose space in relation to the content.

form.title: Form
form.hook: Light and shadow can make a flat drawing suggest depth.
form.goal: Distinguish a two-dimensional shape from an image suggesting three-dimensional volume.

types.label: Flat shape
types.input: A uniform circle does not show a light side or a shaded side.

types.label: Sphere
types.input: Light and shadow suggest a rounded solid.

types.label: Cube
types.input: Visible faces and edges suggest width, height, and depth.

types.label: Cylinder
types.input: Elliptical ends and a shaded side suggest a curved solid.

types.label: Cone
types.input: A pointed top and a curved base suggest a tapered solid.

vocab.meaning: A lighter area on the surface.
A darker area on the surface.
A shadow falling onto another surface.
The three-dimensional extent of a form.
A way of drawing that suggests depth and viewing position.
The outer boundary can stay circular while the interior suggests depth.

lab.label: Move the light source
lab.observation: The outline stays circular. The highlight moves and the darker side changes.

check.question: Which visible features suggest depth in this ball illustration?
choices: The highlight and shaded side.
A changed circular outline.
A different event time.
check.reason: The highlight and shaded side suggest volume within the same circular outline.

form.extension: These are depth cues in a flat image. A rendered illustration has no physical volume; lighting direction, cast shadows, overlap, and perspective should work coherently.

typography.title: Typography
typography.hook: The words can stay the same while their visual voice changes.
typography.goal: Identify letterform families and the spacing that makes text readable.

types.label: Serif
types.input: Small finishing strokes appear on letters in this serif style.

types.label: Sans serif
types.input: The letters have no serifs.

types.label: Script-like
types.input: Sloping, expressive strokes suggest handwriting.

types.label: Display
types.input: A bold, distinctive style is used for a short headline.

types.label: Monospaced
types.input: Each character occupies the same horizontal advance.

vocab.meaning: A small finishing stroke on a letter.
A style without serifs.
Adjusting the space between a particular pair of letters.
Adjusting spacing across a group of letters.
The distance between lines of type.
The guide on which most letters sit.
An enclosed or partly enclosed space in a letter.
The relative thickness of the strokes.
The height of a capital letter above the baseline.
The height of the main body of lowercase letters such as x.
A stroke that rises above the main body of a lowercase letter.
A stroke that extends below the baseline.
A main stroke of a letter.

lab.label: Change the space between lines
lab.observation: The words and type size stay fixed. The line spacing changes.

check.question: Why is generous line spacing useful in this short reading panel?
choices: It helps separate the lines without changing the wording.
It changes a serif into a sans serif.
It makes every character monospaced.
check.reason: The visible gaps separate the lines. This is leading, not a change in letterform family.

typography.extension: Legibility concerns recognising individual characters; readability concerns reading the text comfortably. Body text needs testing at its actual size, spacing, length, and background.

contrast.title: Contrast
contrast.hook: A difference can help one detail stand out. Contrast is more than color.
contrast.goal: Compare differences in value, size, weight, shape, and direction.

types.label: Light–dark contrast
types.input: One dark circle differs from the lighter circles.

types.label: Size contrast
types.input: One large circle differs from the smaller circles.

types.label: Shape contrast
types.input: One square differs from the circles.

types.label: Weight contrast
types.input: One word has heavier strokes than the others.

types.label: Direction contrast
types.input: One line points in a different direction.

vocab.meaning: The visible feature that is not the same.
A light–dark difference.
A big–small difference.
A difference in stroke thickness.
Giving a feature more visual attention.

lab.label: Change the light–dark difference
lab.observation: The wording and size stay fixed. The text becomes more distinct from the background.

check.question: Why is the time easier to locate in the second notice?
choices: Its darker color creates a stronger value difference.
Its meaning has changed.
The whole notice uses identical values.
check.reason: The darker time stands out from the pale background and the supporting text.

contrast.extension: Strong contrast can support hierarchy, but making everything contrast equally creates competition. Use shape, size, and labels as well as color when information must be distinguished.

hierarchy.title: Hierarchy
hierarchy.hook: The reader needs an order: what matters first, next, and after that?
hierarchy.goal: Organise visual importance using more than size alone.

types.label: Size hierarchy
types.input: The largest heading attracts attention before the smaller details.

types.label: Weight hierarchy
types.input: The heavier heading differs from lighter supporting text.

types.label: Color hierarchy
types.input: An accent distinguishes one item from the surrounding information.

types.label: Position hierarchy
types.input: Placement separates the heading from supporting content.

types.label: Space hierarchy
types.input: Extra space isolates the most important message.

vocab.meaning: The message that needs attention first.
Details that support the main message.
Additional supporting detail.
A feature that attracts attention.
A way of making information more prominent.

lab.label: Change the headline size
lab.observation: The heading grows while the supporting details stay the same size.

check.question: What should a reader notice first on this community-event notice?
choices: The event name, followed by the time and place.
Every line with exactly equal emphasis.
The tiny decorative marks before the event name.
check.reason: The headline introduces the event. The supporting details then tell the reader when and where.

hierarchy.extension: Visual order should follow the communication goal. The biggest text is not automatically the right primary message; decide what the audience needs first.

alignment.title: Alignment
alignment.hook: Shared edges and guides help separate pieces feel organised.
alignment.goal: See left, right, centred, justified, and grid-based alignment.

types.label: Left aligned
types.input: The lines begin along the same left edge.

types.label: Right aligned
types.input: The lines end along the same right edge.

types.label: Centred
types.input: The lines share a centre axis.

types.label: Justified
types.input: Most lines reach both edges; the final line can be shorter.

types.label: Grid
types.input: Rows and columns share repeated guides.

vocab.meaning: The side along which elements line up.
The shared middle guide.
Letters can share a common bottom guide.
A system of rows and columns.
A vertical group in a layout.
The space between columns.

lab.label: Bring the text blocks to a shared edge
lab.observation: The wording stays fixed. The starting edges move towards a shared guide.

check.question: Which feature makes these reading blocks look organised?
choices: Their common left edge.
Changing each word to a new language.
Giving each block an unrelated starting point.
check.reason: The blocks line up along one left edge. The shared guide creates a visible connection.

alignment.extension: Alignment does not mean centring everything. Pick guides suited to the content, and use exceptions deliberately rather than scattering every edge.

balance.title: Balance
balance.hook: Visual weight is attention, not physical mass.
balance.goal: Compare symmetrical, asymmetrical, and radial arrangements.

types.label: Symmetrical
types.input: Similar visual weight is mirrored around the centre.

types.label: Asymmetrical
types.input: Different elements can distribute attention across the composition.

types.label: Radial
types.input: Elements are arranged around a central point.

vocab.meaning: How strongly an element attracts attention.
The guide around which an arrangement is mirrored.
Similar arrangements on opposite sides.
Different arrangements on opposite sides.
An arrangement around a centre.
The point or area around which the composition is organised.

lab.label: Change the left shape’s visual weight
lab.observation: The positions stay fixed. The left circle changes size relative to the right circle.

check.question: Why can the second composition feel balanced without being a mirror image?
choices: Different-sized elements distribute visual weight across both sides.
Balance always requires identical objects.
The picture has physical mass on a scale.
check.reason: The arrangement uses different elements on opposite sides. It illustrates asymmetrical balance; visual weight is perceived attention.

balance.extension: Size, darkness, color, detail, and position can all influence visual weight. An asymmetrical arrangement needs judgement and testing, not a physical-weight equation.

proximity.title: Proximity
proximity.hook: A gap can tell the reader which details belong together.
proximity.goal: Distinguish space within a group from space between groups.

types.label: Related pair
types.input: A heading and its detail sit close together.

types.label: Separate groups
types.input: Small internal gaps and a larger external gap suggest two groups.

types.label: Misleading proximity
types.input: An unrelated detail sits close enough to appear connected.

types.label: Image and caption
types.input: The caption sits close to the image it describes.

vocab.meaning: Elements perceived as belonging together.
Information that has a meaningful connection.
Empty space separating elements.
Several elements gathered closely.
Text explaining an image.

lab.label: Bring a heading and its detail together
lab.observation: The two related lines move closer. The gap to the next group stays larger.

check.question: Which gap makes the date and time read as one group?
choices: A small gap between them and a larger gap before the address.
Equal huge gaps between every detail.
Placing the time beside an unrelated caption.
check.reason: The date and time sit close together, while extra space separates the location group.

proximity.extension: Close placement communicates a relationship even when you did not intend one. Check whether the visual grouping matches the actual meaning.

repetition.title: Repetition
repetition.hook: Repeated features can make different messages belong to one system.
repetition.goal: Compare repetition, rhythm, and controlled variation.

types.label: Regular repetition
types.input: The same motif returns at equal intervals.

types.label: Alternating rhythm
types.input: Two features repeat in an A–B–A–B arrangement.

types.label: Progressive rhythm
types.input: A repeated form changes in a regular sequence.

types.label: Consistent identity
types.input: Different cards share selected colors, type, and layout.

vocab.meaning: One visual unit that repeats.
The visible pattern created as features repeat.
Selected features follow the same system.
A controlled difference within a repeated system.
Shared visual features that help messages feel related.

lab.label: Bring the cards into one visual system
lab.observation: The messages remain different. Their color and type treatment become more consistent.

check.question: What connects these three club cards?
choices: The repeated color, headline style, and divider position.
Identical wording on every card.
A different visual style on every card.
check.reason: The content differs, but the same selected design features repeat.

repetition.extension: Repeat useful features, not every detail. Controlled variation can distinguish different messages while keeping a recognisable system.

simplicity.title: Simplicity
simplicity.hook: Remove unnecessary complication while keeping the information people need.
simplicity.goal: Distinguish useful simplicity from a design that is merely empty.

types.label: Cluttered
types.input: Extra marks compete with the event information.

types.label: Essential information
types.input: The event, date, place, and action remain visible.

types.label: Too little information
types.input: Removing the date and place makes this invitation less useful.

types.label: Purposeful detail
types.input: A necessary route or instruction can require more detail.

vocab.meaning: Needed for the message to work.
Competing detail that makes the message harder to find.
Repeated information that adds little here.
A visual addition that may not carry essential information.
What the design needs to help someone do.

lab.label: Remove decorative clutter
lab.observation: Decorative marks disappear. The event name, date, place, and invitation remain.

check.question: Which simplified invitation still works?
choices: The one keeping the event, date, place, and action.
The one showing only the event name.
The one hiding every useful detail.
check.reason: Simplicity preserves the essential message. Fewer elements are not better if needed information disappears.

simplicity.extension: Simplicity is relative to a purpose. A timetable or a map may need more information than a logo; remove unnecessary complexity rather than counting elements.

function.title: Function
function.hook: A design succeeds when its audience can understand or do what it is for.
function.goal: Judge the design by its purpose, audience, context, and action.

types.label: Inform
types.input: A timetable tells people when activities happen.

types.label: Guide
types.input: A sign and an arrow help people find a place.

types.label: Invite
types.input: A poster gives the event, date, place, and next action.

types.label: Support an action
types.input: A clearly labelled control tells someone what to do next.

vocab.meaning: The job the design needs to do.
The people who need to use or understand it.
Where and how someone will see the design.
A clear next step for the viewer.
Individual characters can be recognised.
A visible cue that suggests how something can be used.

lab.label: Simulate seeing the notice from farther away
lab.observation: The notice gets smaller on the screen. Check which details you can still identify.

check.question: Which information lets someone act on this event poster?
choices: The date, place, and clear registration instruction.
Only the decorative circle.
A beautiful headline with no event details.
check.reason: The practical details and the call to action let a viewer decide what to do next.

function.extension: A beautiful design can still fail its purpose. Test it with someone from the intended audience in a realistic viewing or use context.
